text.en: Meena compared two turmeric-paper marks from labelled samples. One stayed yellow and the other turned reddish brown. She wondered what a second test would tell her.

In the Arrhenius model, acids increase the concentration of hydrogen ions in water and bases increase the concentration of hydroxide ions. Use indicator results to classify classroom samples. Bases soluble in water are alkalis. Acids are classed by basicity as monobasic, dibasic and tribasic according to the replaceable hydrogen ions per molecule.
Indicators such as litmus show acids and bases by colour change. In the textbook reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, the products are sodium chloride and water. Neutralisation describes the reaction. The final pH depends on the substances and amounts mixed. Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals because many compounds are made from it.
Salts are classed as normal, acidic and basic, and some crystallise with water of crystallisation, as in copper sulphate. The pH scale describes how acidic or basic an aqueous solution is. Concentration and the extent of ionisation both affect the pH.

In the textbook reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, the products are sodium chloride and water. Neutralisation describes the reaction. The final pH depends on the substances and amounts mixed.
Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals because many compounds are made from it.
Salts are classed as normal, acidic and basic, and some crystallise with water of crystallisation, as in copper sulphate.
The pH scale describes how acidic or basic an aqueous solution is. Concentration and the extent of ionisation both affect the pH.
Lemon juice contains citric acid. That is a familiar example of an acidic material. For a science comparison, a teacher can label samples and use paper indicators.

board.text: Use a labelled sample and indicator

text.en: An Arrhenius acid raises the amount of hydrogen ions in water. In water those ions attach to water molecules, and the simplified equations often write them as H plus.
A base such as sodium hydroxide gives hydroxide ions as it dissolves in water. An alkali is a base that is soluble in water.
An acid can donate one, two or three hydrogen ions per molecule in a neutralisation model. These cases are called monobasic, dibasic and tribasic.
Some hydrogen atoms in a formula are held in positions that do not release hydrogen ions in an ordinary acid reaction. Acetic acid contains four hydrogen atoms but is a monobasic acid.
Compare hydrochloric acid and acetic acid in a particle diagram. At similar stated concentrations, they differ in how much of the acid ionises in water.

board.text: Extent of ionisation distinguishes strong and weak

text.en: Concentration instead describes how much substance is present in a given amount of solution. Water can dilute a strong acid while the acid still belongs to the strong category.

board.text: Concentration and strength describe different properties

text.en: Start with blue and red litmus in a diagram. With an acidic sample, blue turns red. The other strip stays red. One change is enough in this model to support acidity.
A basic sample changes red litmus to blue, while blue litmus stays blue. Both strips keep their colour in a neutral sample under ordinary test conditions.

board.text: Base: red → blue; neutral: both unchanged

text.en: Keep a separate strip for each test. A reused strip may carry material from a previous solution and change the new result.
Turmeric can give a reddish-brown colour in a basic sample. It generally stays yellow in acidic and neutral samples, so choose litmus for another observation when the turmeric stays yellow.

board.text: Yellow turmeric alone cannot distinguish acid and neutral

text.en: The pH scale for familiar water-based samples often runs from zero to fourteen. At ordinary room temperature, seven is neutral. Lower values indicate acidity and higher values indicate basicity.

board.text: Room temperature: pH <7 acid, pH >7 base

text.en: A change of one pH unit corresponds to a tenfold change in hydrogen-ion activity. In a simple dilute-solution comparison, pH four indicates about ten times the hydrogen-ion concentration of pH five.

board.text: One pH unit represents a factor of 10

text.en: An acid and a hydroxide base can react to form water when hydrogen ions combine with hydroxide ions. The remaining ions can make up a salt.
Read the example equation as chemical symbols on the board. Hydrochloric acid supplies hydrogen and chloride ions, and sodium hydroxide supplies sodium and hydroxide ions.
Neither seeing a salt in a formula nor taking part in neutralisation guarantees a neutral final solution. In a mixture with excess acid or base, the excess can determine the final pH.

board.text: Final pH depends on the products and any excess

text.en: A normal salt in this classification has the acidic hydrogen replaced completely. An acid salt retains an acidic hydrogen, as in sodium hydrogencarbonate.

board.text: Normal and acid salts describe how the formula is formed

text.en: A basic salt can retain hydroxide in its formula after partial neutralisation of a base. Treat these salt labels as structural descriptions. A separate test gives the pH of their solutions.

board.text: Structural salt labels differ from pH readings

text.en: Some salts form crystals with water incorporated in a fixed ratio. The water is part of that crystalline structure and is called water of crystallisation.

board.text: Hydrate: salt with water in the crystal structure

text.en: In the textbook example of blue vitriol, five water molecules are written per copper sulphate formula unit. Read the dot in the formula as a way of showing the hydrate.

board.text: CuSO₄·5H₂O: five waters per formula unit

text.en: Common uses depend on the particular salt. Sodium chloride is common table salt, and calcium carbonate occurs in chalk and limestone. Different salts can contain different ions.

board.text: Identify the salt before describing its use

text.en: Compare a pH result with the sample name. An indicator gives evidence of acidity or basicity. Several different solutions can give the same result, so one colour cannot identify a specific chemical.

board.text: Indicator classifies acidity; more evidence identifies a substance

problem.en: A classroom diagram shows blue litmus turning red in sample A and red litmus turning blue in sample B. Which is acidic and which is basic?

text.en: Use the change to red in sample A.

why.en: Blue litmus turns red in an acidic sample.

text.en: Use the change to blue in sample B.

why.en: Red litmus turns blue in a basic sample.

prompt.en: A friend says All bases dissolve in water. How will you reply?

requiredIdeas.en: Those that dissolve are called alkalis.

points.en: Arrhenius acids increase hydrogen ions in water and bases increase hydroxide ions.
Indicators show acids and bases by colour.
pH describes the acidity or basicity of an aqueous solution.
